narrative:
The model determined that you have a 95.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and this predicted failure rate is so high, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Your first-year class ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward not passing. Your LSAT score came third and further increased the likelihood of failure.

In each case the direction was the same: all three features moved the prediction away from success and toward bar exam failure. Compared with students who were accepted, your first-year ranking placed you in the second decile while accepted students averaged the sixth decile. Your third-year ranking was even lower, in the bottom decile, while accepted students averaged near the sixth. Your LSAT of 28 also sat well below the 37-point average of admitted students. These academic performance signals were simply too far from the typical profile of students who pass the bar for the model to predict success.

You should focus on strengthening the areas the model weighed most heavily. Retaking the LSAT, improving your study habits to raise future grades, and seeking structured bar-prep support could meaningfully change your trajectory before you reapply.
